title: The Supreme Court Just Told 250,000 Babies a Year They're Still American. Here's What It Means for H-1B Families.
excerpt: In a 6-3 ruling on the final day of its term, the court struck down Trump's executive order restricting birthright citizenship — a case that had Indian professionals on temporary visas watching closer than anyone.
body:
The US Supreme Court on Tuesday struck down President Donald Trump's executive order restricting birthright citizenship, ruling 6-3 that virtually all children born on American soil are citizens under the 14th Amendment — regardless of their parents' immigration status.

The decision in *Trump v. Barbara*, handed down on the final day of the court's term, ends a legal battle that had gripped the Indian diaspora for over a year. For the hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals in the United States on H-1B visas — many stuck in green card backlogs stretching decades — the ruling removes what had become an existential threat to their families.

"Citizenship, then and now, was the right to have rights — to freely participate in our political community," Chief Justice John Roberts wrote for the majority. "The Framers of the Fourteenth Amendment extended that promise to every free-born person in this land. We keep that promise today."

## What Trump's order would have done

Trump signed Executive Order 14160 on his first day back in office in January 2025. It directed federal agencies to stop recognising the citizenship of children born in the United States if neither parent was a US citizen or lawful permanent resident. Under the policy, babies born to H-1B holders, F-1 students, J-1 exchange visitors, and other temporary visa holders — as well as undocumented immigrants — would have received only derivative immigration status tied to their parents.

The Migration Policy Institute estimated the order would have affected roughly 255,000 babies born on US soil each year — about 6 per cent of all projected births.

For Indian families, the stakes were acute. Indians are the largest group of H-1B visa holders in the United States, and many live in the country for years — sometimes more than a decade — while waiting for employment-based green cards. Their children, born in American hospitals, attend American schools, and have known no other home. Under Trump's order, those children would have been classified as H-4 dependents rather than citizens, their status contingent entirely on their parents' visa.


![President Donald Trump — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/13/Official_Presidential_Portrait_of_President_Donald_J._Trump_%282025%29_%28cropped%29%282%29.jpg)



> **""Citizenship, then and now, was the right to have rights — to freely participate in our political community," Chief Justice John Roberts wrote for the majority."**



## How the court ruled

Roberts, joined by Justices Amy Coney Barrett, Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan, and Ketanji Brown Jackson, held that the 14th Amendment's Citizenship Clause — "All persons born or naturalized in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof, are citizens" — means exactly what it says.

The majority drew heavily on the landmark 1898 ruling in *United States v. Wong Kim Ark*, which held that a man born in San Francisco to Chinese immigrant parents was a US citizen. Roberts wrote that in the 128 years since that decision, "we have repeatedly understood the rule of Wong Kim Ark to guarantee citizenship to all children born in the United States and subject to its power. We see no reason to depart from that view today."

The court rejected the Trump administration's argument that "subject to the jurisdiction thereof" required permanent domicile or "direct and immediate allegiance." Roberts called the revisionist interpretation unsupported: "The trouble is that there is scant evidence for this dramatically revisionist view."

Justice Brett Kavanaugh provided the crucial sixth vote to strike down the order but broke with the majority's constitutional reasoning. He argued the executive order was not unconstitutional but conflicted with a federal statute — 8 USC §1401(a) — that grants citizenship at birth in language mirroring the 14th Amendment. In Kavanaugh's view, Congress could theoretically change that statute without violating the Constitution, but it has not done so.

The three dissenters — Justices Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito, and Neil Gorsuch — argued the majority had misread the 14th Amendment. Alito called it "one of the most important decisions in the history of the Court" and warned of "grotesque results," including citizenship for children of "birth tourists."

## What it means for Indian families


![Chief Justice John Roberts — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/43/Official_roberts_CJ.jpg)


The ruling settles a question that had consumed Indian professional communities across the United States since January 2025. During oral arguments in April, South Asian American advocacy groups rallied outside the court, and organisations like the South Asian American Joint Congress of Organizations filed amicus briefs warning that thousands of babies born to Indian H-1B holders could be rendered effectively stateless — since India does not automatically grant citizenship to children born abroad.

The practical impact is immediate. Indian families on temporary visas can continue to obtain US passports and Social Security numbers for their American-born children. The spectre of children being classified as H-4 dependents — subject to deportation if their parents lost visa status — is gone.

But the ruling does not resolve the deeper structural problem facing Indian professionals: a green card backlog so severe that an Indian-born applicant filing today in the EB-2 category could wait 50 years or more. While their children's citizenship is now secure, the parents themselves remain in immigration limbo.

## A consequential term ends

The birthright citizenship ruling capped a Supreme Court term packed with major decisions. On Monday, the court blocked Trump from firing Federal Reserve Board member Lisa Cook but expanded presidential power over independent agencies more broadly. Earlier in the term, it rejected Trump's sweeping global tariffs, gutted a key provision of the Voting Rights Act, and expanded gun rights.

On Tuesday, alongside the birthright ruling, the court also allowed states to ban transgender student athletes from women's sports teams in a 9-0 decision on the statutory question, and struck down federal limits on coordinated spending between political parties and candidates.

The ACLU, which represented the plaintiffs in *Trump v. Barbara*, called birthright citizenship "foundational to who we are as a nation." The advocacy group Stop AAPI Hate welcomed the ruling but warned the administration would try other avenues. "Their attack on birthright citizenship is just one part of their broader plan to make America permanently hostile to people of colour," the group said.

For the Indian diaspora — which numbers over 4.4 million in the United States — Tuesday's ruling is less a victory than a confirmation: their children, born on American soil, are American. The Constitution, the court said, has always said so.

**Sources:** Reuters, Wall Street Journal, USA Today, New York Post, Barron's, Migration Policy Institute
